# `secrets/provider-key`: Hardcoded provider credential

<!-- Generated by `npm run docs:rules` from the rule metadata in src/rules/. Edit only the
     hand:* regions here; everything else comes from the rule and is overwritten. -->

| Family  | Default severity | GitHub security-severity | CWE                                                                                                                    |
| ------- | ---------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| secrets | critical         | 9.5                      | [CWE-798](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html), [CWE-312](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/312.html) |

Individual findings can have a lower or higher severity than the default, and each has a
confidence (high, medium or low). Both are explained below.

## What it detects

<!-- hand:detects -->

Literal credentials whose format identifies the provider, in any scanned text file (code,
config, YAML, JSON, committed `.env` files):

- Stripe live secret and restricted keys; OpenAI and Anthropic API keys; SendGrid keys;
  GitHub classic and fine-grained tokens; Supabase `service_role` JWTs (decoded locally,
  `role` claim) and `sb_secret_` keys: **critical**.
- AWS secret access keys (when named as such), Slack tokens, Twilio API keys, Resend keys:
  **high** or **critical**. AWS access key IDs are reported at **high** with medium
  confidence: an ID alone is not a secret, but its secret key is usually nearby.
- Google API keys (**medium**; escalated to critical when the context shows a Gemini /
  Generative Language key), Slack incoming webhooks (**medium**).
- Database connection strings with an embedded password (`postgres://user:pass@host`).

Stripe test-mode keys are reported separately by
[`secrets/provider-key-test`](provider-key-test.md) at low severity.

<!-- /hand:detects -->

## Why it matters

A credential for a third-party service (Stripe, OpenAI, AWS, Supabase, GitHub, a database, …) is written directly in a file that is, or will be, committed. Anyone with read access to the repository, its history, a fork, a CI log or a client bundle can use it. Deleting the line later does not remove it from git history.

## Messages

What a finding from this rule says (parameters in braces):

- {provider} is hardcoded in this file.
- {provider} is hardcoded. On its own it is an identifier, but its secret key is usually nearby; check this file and its history.
- A database connection string with an embedded password is hardcoded.

## How to fix

1. Revoke and rotate the credential in the provider dashboard now; assume it is compromised.
2. Load it from an environment variable on the server only (never with a NEXT_PUBLIC_/VITE_ prefix).
3. Keep real values in a gitignored .env.local or your host’s secret manager, and commit only a .env.example with placeholders.
4. If it was pushed, purge it from history (git filter-repo) after rotating.

### Vulnerable

```ts
// src/lib/stripe.ts
import Stripe from 'stripe';
export const stripe = new Stripe('sk_live_…'); // real key committed to git
```

### Fixed

```ts
// src/lib/stripe.ts (server-only module)
import 'server-only';
import Stripe from 'stripe';

const key = process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY;
if (!key) throw new Error('STRIPE_SECRET_KEY is not set');
export const stripe = new Stripe(key);

// .env.local (gitignored):   STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=<from the Stripe dashboard>
// .env.example (committed):  STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=
```

## False positives and limitations

<!-- hand:false-positives -->

- **Documented example values** (the keys published in AWS, Stripe and other vendor docs)
  and obvious placeholders (`your-key-here`, `xxxx`, `<KEY>`, repeated characters,
  low-entropy look-alikes) are never reported.
- **Public-by-design keys are not reported:** the Supabase anon / `sb_publishable_` key and
  Firebase web `apiKey` values in `initializeApp({...})`.
- **Well-known default database passwords** (`postgres:postgres@localhost`, docker-compose
  service passwords) are not reported.
- **Gitignored, untracked env files** (such as `.env.local`) are not checked for hardcoded
  secrets, because that is where local secrets belong.
- **Test files:** matches in test code are kept, with confidence lowered one step. Real
  keys do get pasted into integration tests.
- **Limitations:** no validity check (VibeGuard never contacts providers, so a revoked key
  looks the same as a live one); secrets that are concatenated, encoded or built at runtime
  are missed; formats not in the signature list fall back to
  [`secrets/high-entropy`](high-entropy.md); git history is not scanned.

<!-- /hand:false-positives -->

## How to suppress

Only suppress a finding after confirming it is safe. Put the directive on the line above
the reported line (or use `vibeguard-ignore-line` on the line itself, or
`vibeguard-ignore-file` anywhere in the file). The reason is required: a directive without
one suppresses nothing and is reported.

```ts
// vibeguard-ignore-next-line secrets/provider-key -- explain why this is safe (at least 10 characters)
<the line VibeGuard reported>
```

Use the comment syntax of the file: `//` or `/* */` in code, `#` in `.env` and YAML
files, `--` in SQL.

To turn the rule off or change its severity for the whole project, use `.vibeguard.yml`:

```yaml
version: 1
rules:
  secrets/provider-key: off # or: { severity: low }
```

See [configuration](../../configuration.md) and
[ADR-0004](../../adr/0004-suppression-design.md).

## CWE

- [CWE-798](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html): Use of Hard-coded Credentials
- [CWE-312](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/312.html): Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information
